LESSON 3 OF 106·Cyber Security Fundamentals

The CIA Triad: Confidentiality, Integrity & Availability

Availability, integrity, confidentiality — three questions you can ask about any system, and the reason improving one usually costs you another.

Beginner3 min
Why this matters

Confidentiality, integrity and availability are the three questions you can ask about any system. They are not a checklist to pass; they are a way to find out which one you have been ignoring.

What you'll learn

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • name the three goals and the question each one asks
  • look at a real account and say which goal is weakest
  • explain why improving one goal can make another worse

In plain English

Ask three questions about any piece of information, and you have the whole of the CIA triad. They are short enough to memorise, and they cover almost every security failure you will ever read about.

Here they are, in the order that makes them easiest to remember:

  • Can the people who need it get it, when they need it? That is availability.
  • Is it still correct, and did it arrive unchanged? That is integrity.
  • Has anyone else seen it, or could they? That is confidentiality.

Most people think of security as the third question only — keeping secrets. The other two cause more visible damage, more often.

How it works

The three goals pull against each other, and that tension is the useful part.

  • More backups improve availability, but every extra copy is another place the data can leak from — so confidentiality gets harder.
  • More access checks improve confidentiality, but a bad access rule can lock out the person who needs the data at 3am — so availability suffers.
  • Faster sync improves availability, but if it copies a corrupted value everywhere before anyone notices, integrity suffers.

Good security is not maximising all three. It is deciding, for this particular system, which one you would sacrifice first — and writing that decision down so it is a decision and not an accident.

A worked example

Your bank account, failure by failure:

  • The balance shows 0 because a transfer posted twice. Availability is fine, confidentiality is fine, integrity is broken. You can log in and see a wrong number.
  • The app will not load on payday. Availability is broken, the other two are intact.
  • Your statement is visible inside someone else's app after a bug. Confidentiality is broken, and the other two look perfectly normal — which is why this one can go unnoticed for months.

Three different failures, three different responses. A plan that only ever asks "is it secret?" has no answer for the first two.

The mistake most beginners make

Assuming confidentiality is the only goal, so any problem that does not involve a leak is not a security problem. A hospital whose records cannot be opened during an emergency is having a security incident, whether or not anything leaked.

The second mistake is assuming you can improve all three for free. You cannot; every control you add trades one against another, and the job is to know which trade you made.

Try it in two minutes

Take one account you use every day — email is a good choice — and answer three questions honestly:

  • If it were unavailable for a day, what would break?
  • If one message were silently changed, would you notice?
  • Who else could read it right now, including the provider?

Whichever answer made you least comfortable is the goal to work on. For most people it is the third, and the fix is usually two-factor authentication rather than anything more complicated.

Practice / apply

Choose one account you use daily and answer the three questions about it on paper. No tools, no sign-in needed.

Key takeaways

  • Availability: can the right people get it? Integrity: is it still correct? Confidentiality: who else can see it?
  • Confidentiality is the goal people think of first and the one whose failures are noticed last.
  • The three goals trade against each other; a control that improves one usually costs another.
  • Decide which goal you would sacrifice first, deliberately, and write it down.
